title: How do you approach a broad "Design X" (e.g. Netflix) question in an interview — decompose by user journeys into independent components, then follow Requirement → Responsibility → Data → Technology (and only introduce Redis/Kafka/CDN/sharding where a real bottleneck justifies it) rather than Technology-first?
shortTitle: How do you approach a broad "Design X" question in an interview?

s1_definition.profdef: Approaching a broad "Design X" question means driving the design top-down from what the system must do rather than bottom-up from technologies you want to name-drop. You first clarify and scope the requirements, both functional (what features) and non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency), then you decompose the system by user journeys into independent components, and for each component you follow a disciplined chain: Requirement (what must this part achieve), then Responsibility (what single job this component owns), then Data (what it stores and reads and how much), and only then Technology (the concrete database, cache, queue, or CDN). Critically, you introduce a specific technology like Redis, Kafka, a CDN, or sharding only at the point where a real, named bottleneck justifies it, so every technology choice is defended by a number or a constraint rather than by fashion. This keeps the design coherent, shows the interviewer your reasoning, and avoids the classic failure of jumping straight to a buzzword-laden architecture that solves problems you never established exist.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India asks you to "design a new branch." The weak approach is to immediately shout "put in a huge vault, a fleet of armored trucks, and ten ATMs!" before anyone has said how many customers come or what they do. The strong approach is to first ask who uses the branch and what they come to do — deposit, withdraw, apply for loans — then for each of those customer journeys you ask what that counter needs to achieve, what single job each counter owns, what paperwork and records it handles and how much, and only then do you decide whether this counter needs a small cash drawer or a bank vault, one clerk or ten, a filing cabinet or a whole archive. You add the armored truck only when you can say "we move fifty crore rupees a day, so we need it." Every expensive thing is justified by a real need you established first.
s1_definition.oneliner: Decompose a "Design X" question by user journeys into components, and for each one reason Requirement then Responsibility then Data then Technology, introducing Redis, Kafka, a CDN, or sharding only where a named bottleneck proves it is needed, never technology-first.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Approaching a broad "Design X" question means driving the design top-down from what the system must do rather than bottom-up from technologies you want to name-drop. You first clarify and scope the requirements, both functional (what features) and non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency), then you decompose the system by user journeys into independent components, and for each component you follow a disciplined chain: Requirement (what must this part achieve), then Responsibility (what single job this component owns), then Data (what it stores and reads and how much), and only then Technology (the concrete database, cache, queue, or CDN). Critically, you introduce a specific technology like Redis, Kafka, a CDN, or sharding only at the point where a real, named bottleneck justifies it, so every technology choice is defended by a number or a constraint rather than by fashion. This keeps the design coherent, shows the interviewer your reasoning, and avoids the classic failure of jumping straight to a buzzword-laden architecture that solves problems you never established exist.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India asks you to "design a new branch." The weak approach is to immediately shout "put in a huge vault, a fleet of armored trucks, and ten ATMs!" before anyone has said how many customers come or what they do. The strong approach is to first ask who uses the branch and what they come to do — deposit, withdraw, apply for loans — then for each of those customer journeys you ask what that counter needs to achieve, what single job each counter owns, what paperwork and records it handles and how much, and only then do you decide whether this counter needs a small cash drawer or a bank vault, one clerk or ten, a filing cabinet or a whole archive. You add the armored truck only when you can say "we move fifty crore rupees a day, so we need it." Every expensive thing is justified by a real need you established first.

**One line to remember:** Decompose a "Design X" question by user journeys into components, and for each one reason Requirement then Responsibility then Data then Technology, introducing Redis, Kafka, a CDN, or sharding only where a named bottleneck proves it is needed, never technology-first.

sections.s2_technical:
The first phase is requirements and scoping, and skipping it is the most common interview failure. You ask clarifying questions to bound the problem: which features are in scope (for a Netflix-style system, is it browsing and streaming, or also recommendations, billing, and uploads?), who the users are, and what the scale is. You then separate functional requirements (play a video, search the catalog, resume where you left off) from non-functional requirements (how many concurrent streams, acceptable startup latency, availability target like four or five nines, and consistency needs). You do a quick back-of-envelope estimate here — daily active users times actions gives queries per second, content size times catalog gives storage — because those numbers are what later justify each technology. Writing the scope on the board and getting the interviewer to agree is what turns an impossibly broad question into a tractable one.

The second phase is decomposition by user journeys. Rather than inventing an abstract box diagram, you walk through what a real user does and let that reveal the independent components. For a streaming system the journeys are: a user signs up and logs in (so there is an account and auth component), browses and searches the catalog (a catalog and search component), presses play and streams a video (a playback and content-delivery component), and the system tracks viewing to resume and recommend (a viewing-history and recommendation component). Each journey exposes one or more components, and because the journeys are largely independent, the components can be separate services that scale independently. This is far stronger than a technology-first diagram because it guarantees you have covered the real use cases and nothing extraneous.

The third phase, done per component, is the Requirement-Responsibility-Data-Technology chain. For each component you first restate its requirement in one sentence (the catalog component must let users search and browse millions of titles with sub-second latency). Then you name its single responsibility (it owns the searchable catalog metadata, nothing else). Then you reason about its data (how many titles, how large each metadata record, read-heavy or write-heavy, what query patterns — search by title, filter by genre). Only then do you choose technology, and you justify it with the data: because it is search-heavy over millions of records with text matching, a search engine like Elasticsearch fits, backed by a relational source of truth. This order ensures every technology is a conclusion, not a starting assumption.

The discipline that most impresses interviewers is introducing infrastructure only at a proven bottleneck. You start each component with the simplest thing that could work — an application server and a relational database — and then you ask "what breaks as we scale?" and introduce a technology to fix that specific break. You add a cache like Redis when you identify that the same data is read far more than written and the database read load is the bottleneck, and you size the cache from the hot fraction. You add a message queue like Kafka when you identify that a write burst must be absorbed or that producers and consumers must be decoupled so a slow downstream does not block the user. You add a CDN when you compute that serving large media from the origin would saturate bandwidth or that users are geographically distributed and latency from a single region is too high — for video this is immediate because the content is huge and global. You add sharding when you compute that the data or the write throughput exceeds a single node. Each of these is defended by a number: "we serve petabytes of video to a global audience, so a CDN at the edge is mandatory," not "let's add a CDN because Netflix has one."

The fourth phase is addressing the non-functional requirements across the whole design: availability (replication, multiple regions, failover), consistency (where you need strong consistency like billing versus where eventual consistency is fine like view counts), and the inevitable bottlenecks. You walk the critical path of the main user journey and check its latency against the latency numbers every engineer knows, confirming that you have kept slow operations like cross-region calls off that path. You discuss the single points of failure and how each is eliminated. And you call out the trade-offs you are making explicitly, because every senior design is a set of trade-offs, and naming them shows maturity.

A senior nuance is to timebox and go breadth-first, then deepen where the interviewer steers. You sketch the whole picture at a shallow level first so the interviewer sees you can scope the entire system, then you dive deep into the one or two components they are most interested in. Another nuance is to distinguish the read path from the write path, because they usually have very different scale and consistency needs and often completely different technologies — for streaming, the write path (uploading and encoding content) is low volume and batch, while the read path (streaming to millions) is enormous and latency-sensitive, and conflating them produces a muddled design. The overarching message is that a good system design is a story that flows from requirements to responsibilities to data to technology, where the interviewer can follow every decision and challenge it, rather than a pile of trendy components assembled before the problem was understood.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India asks a candidate to "design the mobile banking app backend," and the architect works through it methodically instead of jumping to technologies.

Problem 1 — The architect must not start by naming databases and queues. First she scopes: which journeys are in scope — login, check balance and transactions, transfer money, pay bills? And what scale — ten million daily users? This is the requirements-and-scoping phase.

Problem 2 — She decomposes by user journey into components: an auth component for login, an accounts component for balances and history, a transfer component for moving money, and a notifications component for alerts. Each journey reveals a component with one clear responsibility. This is the decompose-by-journey phase.

Problem 3 — For each component she reasons Requirement, then Responsibility, then Data, then Technology, and introduces Redis only where balance reads dominate, Kafka only where transfer events must fan out to notifications without blocking the user, and sharding only if the transaction store exceeds one node. This is the justify-technology-at-a-bottleneck phase.

We will model a design assistant that takes a system brief, decomposes it into components by user journey, and for each component runs the Requirement-Responsibility-Data-Technology chain, deciding whether to introduce a cache, a queue, a CDN, or sharding based on named thresholds, and printing a defensible design.

The code will have a `UserJourney` and a derived `Component`, a `DesignDecision` capturing the chosen technology and its justification, a `DesignAssistant` that applies the Requirement-Responsibility-Data-Technology chain and threshold rules, and a demo that designs the mobile banking backend journey by journey.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a brief to design a mobile banking backend for 10 million daily users, broken into four user journeys with their read and write rates, dataset sizes, and whether they serve media.

Step 1 — The assistant records the scope and that the design will proceed by user journey, not by technology. No components exist yet; it has only the brief.

Step 2 — It takes the login journey. Requirement: verify credentials and issue tokens. Responsibility: auth only. Data: 20,000 reads versus 4,000 writes, 8 gigabytes. The read-write ratio is 5 to 1, which meets the cache threshold, so it adds Redis for session and token reads, and the 8 gigabytes is under the shard threshold so no sharding. The technology is now justified by a number.

Step 3 — It takes the check-balance journey. Data: 90,000 reads versus 10,000 writes, 400 gigabytes. The ratio of 9 to 1 justifies Redis for hot balances, and the 400 gigabytes exceeds the single-node limit so it adds sharding. Each addition is tied to a specific bottleneck.

Step 4 — It takes the transfer journey. Data: write-heavy at 20,000 writes. The read-write ratio does not justify a cache, so none is added, but transfers must fan out events to notifications and audit without blocking the user, so it adds Kafka, and the 500-gigabyte store exceeds the limit so it shards. Notably it did not add a cache just because other components had one.

Step 5 — It takes the statements journey. It serves large PDF documents to globally distributed users, which is media-heavy, so it adds a CDN to serve at the edge and spare origin bandwidth, and the 2-terabyte document store is sharded. The CDN appears exactly where media and global users justify it, and nowhere else.

Step 6 — The result is a coherent design where every technology — Redis, Kafka, CDN, sharding — appears only at a component with a named, numeric bottleneck, and the reasoning chain for each is printed so an interviewer can follow and challenge it.

```
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO] === Phase 1: scope — mobile banking backend, 10M DAU ===
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO] === Phase 2: decompose by user journey into components ===
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO] ── Component: auth (journey: login) ──
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO]    Technology:     Spring Boot service + PostgreSQL (source of truth) + Redis cache
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO]    Justified by:   baseline: simplest thing that works; read/write ratio 5:1 ≥ 5 → cache hot reads
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO] ── Component: accounts (journey: check-balance) ──
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO]    Technology:     Spring Boot service + PostgreSQL (source of truth) + Redis cache + sharding
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO]    Justified by:   ...; read/write ratio 9:1 ≥ 5 → cache; dataset 400 GB > 64 GB → shard
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO] ── Component: transfer (journey: transfer-money) ──
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO]    Technology:     Spring Boot service + PostgreSQL (source of truth) + Kafka + sharding
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO]    Justified by:   ...; transfer must fan out events without blocking user; 500 GB > 64 → shard
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO] ── Component: documents (journey: statements) ──
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO]    Technology:     Spring Boot service + PostgreSQL (source of truth) + CDN + sharding
2026-10-24 17:20:44 [INFO]    Justified by:   ...; media-heavy + global users → CDN; 2000 GB > 64 → shard
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I get a broad "Design X" question I drive the design top-down from what the system must do, not bottom-up from technologies I want to name. The most common failure is jumping straight to Redis, Kafka, and a CDN before anyone has established the problem, so I deliberately slow down and scope first. I ask clarifying questions to bound the features in scope, separate functional requirements like play a video or transfer money from non-functional ones like scale, latency, availability, and consistency, and I do a quick back-of-envelope estimate, because those numbers are exactly what will later justify each technology choice.

Then I decompose by user journey rather than drawing an abstract box diagram. I walk through what a real user does — signs up, browses, presses play, and the system tracks viewing — and each journey reveals an independent component with one clear responsibility. This guarantees I have covered the real use cases and nothing extraneous, and because the journeys are largely independent the components can scale separately.

For each component I follow a strict chain: Requirement, then Responsibility, then Data, then Technology. I restate the component's requirement in one sentence, name its single responsibility, reason about its data — how much, read-heavy or write-heavy, what query patterns — and only then do I choose the technology, defended by that data. The discipline that most impresses interviewers is that I start each component with the simplest thing that works, an app server and a relational database, and then introduce infrastructure only at a named bottleneck. I add Redis when reads greatly outnumber writes and the database read load is the bottleneck. I add Kafka when a write burst must be absorbed or events must fan out without blocking the user. I add a CDN when the content is large media served to a global audience. I add sharding when the data or write throughput exceeds a single node. Every one of those is defended by a number, never by fashion.

In my banking work this is exactly how I designed a mobile banking backend. I scoped it to login, balance, transfer, and statements for ten million daily users, decomposed by those journeys into auth, accounts, transfer, and documents components, and then justified each technology: Redis on the read-heavy balance component, Kafka on the transfer component because it must fan out to notifications and audit without blocking the customer, a CDN only on the statements component because it serves large PDFs to global users, and sharding wherever the data exceeded one node. Critically I did not add a cache to the transfer component just because the others had one, because its write-heavy profile did not justify it.

I finish by covering the non-functional requirements across the whole design — replication and multi-region for availability, strong consistency for money movement versus eventual consistency for view counts and notifications, and the single points of failure and how each is removed — and I name my trade-offs explicitly, because every senior design is a set of trade-offs. I go breadth-first so the interviewer sees I can scope the whole system, then I deepen wherever they steer me. The overarching message I leave them with is that a good design is a story that flows from requirements to responsibilities to data to technology, where every decision can be followed and challenged, not a pile of trendy components assembled before the problem was understood.
